name: small_queue (circular-buffer queue with local buffer)
listed_description: Fixed-size power-of-two circular buffer queue of ints stored inside the object, using bitmask indexing instead of modulo; push fails when full.
claim_text: Book table: std::queue<int> 472 ns per iteration (67.8M items/s) versus small_queue 100 ns (319.9M items/s).
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, push and pop of a few ints per iteration, std::queue<int> versus small_queue; compiler, flags and CPU not stated in this chunk.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10 (Local buffer optimization), section 'Small queue'

name: small_vector (local buffer optimization)
listed_description: Vector-like container that keeps a small number of ints in an inline buffer and switches to heap storage when larger, tagging the mode through the size field.
claim_text: Roughly 10x gains in creating and copying small vectors, more with multiple threads (no table shown in this chunk).
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark similar to the small string benchmark: create and copy small vectors, single and multi-threaded, against std::vector; machine and flags not stated here.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10 (Local buffer optimization), section 'Small vector'

name: smartptr_te_lb (type-erased smart pointer with local-buffer deleter)
listed_description: Smart pointer whose deleter type is erased but stored in a 16-byte inline buffer when it fits, avoiding the second allocation of the plain type-erased version.
claim_text: Construct and destroy: 21.0 ns static-deleter pointer, 44.2 ns type-erased, 22.3 ns type-erased with local buffer.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark creating and destroying a pointer to a new int with a trivial deleter; compiler, flags and CPU not stated.
guessed_baseline: type-erased smart pointer with heap-allocated deleter (shared_ptr style)
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10 (Local buffer optimization), section 'Type-erased and callable objects'

name: Type-erased local buffer with vtable (Buffer<S, A> class)
listed_description: General aligned inline buffer that stores any small object and keeps a static vtable of copy, move and delete functions to reconstruct the stored type at run time.
claim_text: Copying a trivially copyable lambda: 5.45 ns without type erasure versus 4.02 ns with the vtable-based version.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark copying a lambda with a captured reference through both buffer implementations; book calls the type-erasure overhead modest. Compiler and CPU not stated.
guessed_baseline: same buffer without type erasure; std::any or std::function style small-object storage
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 10, section 'Local buffer optimization in detail'

name: Template ScopeGuard (non-type-erased)
listed_description: ScopeGuard class template that stores the on-exit callable by type, so the compiler can inline it; contrasted with a std::function-based type-erased guard.
claim_text: Template guard matches explicit delete (4.50 vs 4.48 ns; 4.56 vs 4.54 ns); std::function guard 6.29 ns and 13.4 ns.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark of rand() plus guarded delete, null-pointer case and always-allocate case; explicit delete, std::function guard, buffer-based type-erased guard and template guard compared. Compiler and CPU not stated.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 11, section 'Type-erased ScopeGuard'

name: Type-erased ScopeGuard with fixed inline buffer
listed_description: Type-erased ScopeGuard that requires the callable to fit in a 16-byte inline buffer and calls it through a function pointer, avoiding std::function.
claim_text: Buffer-based guard 5.48 ns versus std::function guard 6.29 ns; 12.7 ns versus 13.4 ns when always allocating.
book_benchmark: Same Google Benchmark as the template ScopeGuard rows; explicit delete baseline 4.48 ns and 4.54 ns. Compiler and CPU not stated.
found_in: book: Hands-On Design Patterns with C++, 2nd ed. (2023), ch. 11, section 'Type-erased ScopeGuard'
